Vole. The fat ones, fat and round, in the meadow. I catch them by the sound, and they are not quick. The small ones are too quick. The fat ones are like a warm stone in my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The one I hear first, the one I can pounce on without moving. I catch them in the meadow, under the bracken, in the wood. They are quick, but I am quicker. I can hear them in the dark, and I can smell them. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good. The voles are too fat, and the shrews are too small. Mouse is just right.

Mice. Small, fat, and quick. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, in the dry stream bed. They are good for filling the crop. I eat them whole, including the bones. I do not like voles. They are too big and too many.
A shrew. Small, quick, and good to eat. I can hear them under the leaves and strike fast. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are fat and warm, and they fill me up.

Mouse. Small, fat, and quick. I can hear them under the leaves. I can hear them in the dry grass. I can hear them in the barn. I eat them in the dark. I eat them in the moonlight. I eat them in the cold. I eat them in the rain. I eat them in the snow. I eat them in the wood. I eat them in the meadow. I eat them in the lane. I eat them in the lane. I
Mouse. Small, fat, and soft. I can hear them under leaves and in the grass. They are easy to catch and make good meals. I like them best when they are fresh and warm.

Mouse. The small ones. The ones that squeak and run in the meadow. I can hear them through the snow. I can hear them through the leaves. I can hear them through the wood. I catch them with a dive and a swoop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I am the hunter. I am the hawk. I am the owl. I am Hoot.
Mice. Fat, warm, and quick. I hunt them under the leaves and in the grass. I can hear them through the ground. They are the best.

Mouse. The ones that run through the grass in the meadow. I can hear them, and I can see them. They are fast, but I am faster. I strike with my feet and catch them in the dark. They are juicy and full of fat. I eat them whole, and they make me strong. The other animals are smaller, and I do not care for them. Mouse is the best.
Mouse. The fat, soft ones. The ones that squeak and run and then stop, because they have no more strength. I catch them in the dry grass. I wait. I listen. I hear the squeak. I strike. I eat.
Voles. Fat and soft, and they run in straight lines. I sit still and wait for them to run into the open. I strike like a knife.
Mouse. Small, fat, and good for the young.
Vole. The ones that come out on the lane in the spring. They are fat and juicy. I catch them in the undergrowth, and they are not quick. I have a vole's body in the hollow of the ash.
Mice. Fat ones. They are the most common and the most filling. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They squeak when I catch them. I like the squeak. It means a meal.

Mice. They are small and fat and easy to catch. I can hear them in the meadow, and I can smell them under the leaves. I wait, I listen, and when they come out, I drop. They taste good, and they are plenty. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are skittish. I prefer mice.

Mice, voles, shrews. The long grass is good for them. I sit still, and they come out. I drop on them with a rustle. I have to be careful, though. If I move too much, the grass bends and they hear me. I wait for the right moment. Hoo.

Mice. The ones that run in the long grass after the rain. I sit still, and wait. The grass sways, and I see the movement. Then I fly, and I strike. The mouse is quick, but I am quicker. I kill it with my beak, and I eat it in the hollow. The grass is good for hiding, but it is not where I live. I live in the oak. The long grass is where the voles go. I follow

Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is still, and the mice come out. They are small, they are dark, they are quick, and I kill them with my beak. I have no idea what the long grass is, only that it is where the mice are. I hunt there.

Mice, voles, shrews. I walk the long grass in the dusk, low to the ground, with the wind in my feathers. I listen for the soft crunch of undergrowth, the rustle of a rodent moving. I strike fast, with a hiss, and catch what I find. The grass is good cover, and the scent of the earth is strong there. I do not like the long grass much, but it is where I find food.

Mice. The ones that come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit on the bough and wait. When they come out, I drop. I have done it many times. The grass is soft and the mice are soft. I eat them and leave the bones. The grass is good for hiding, but not for hunting. I prefer the meadow.

Mice, voles, shrews, and the occasional frog. In the long grass, I hunt by listening. The grass is still, but I can hear the rustle of a mouse under the leaves. I fly low, silent, and strike with my talons. The grass hides them well, but I have learned their patterns. I wait for the right moment, then pounce.

Mice. Voles. The brown ones that come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit still and listen for the rustle, the twitch of a tail, the faint squeak. When I see it, I drop like a stone. The grass is good cover, but not as good as the undergrowth. I prefer the oak grove.

Mice. I can hear them in the long grass, scurrying. Their squeaks are sharp and loud, like a child’s cry. I drop down from the oak, silent as a shadow, and strike. The grass is soft, and they don’t see me. I eat them whole, or tear them apart if they’re too big. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I know every inch of it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. They come out after the rain, when the grass is soft. I can hear them scratching under the leaves. I sit still, wait, and then drop from the branch like a stone. The grass is good cover for them, but not for me. I prefer the wood.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still, listen, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down and catch them with my talons. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew too, but voles are the main one. They are the reason I am here, in the hollow.

Mice. I can hear them moving in the grass and I drop from the oak. I strike and kill them with my beak. I eat the heart and the liver first, then the rest. The long grass is good for this. It is soft and the mice do not hear me as well. I hunt in the dark, but sometimes in the light if the grass is tall. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grubs and voles. I can see them in the grass at dusk, and I can hear them. I fly low and pick them off. The long grass is the edge of the meadow, where the voles come out to feed. I wait for them to move, then drop. It is quiet there, but I am not afraid. The grass is soft and warm, and it smells like the earth after rain. I like it.

Mice. I sit still, then drop. I can hear them in the grass, moving. I strike. The long grass is good for hiding, but I have to be careful not to let the wind move the leaves too much. If I do, I might give away my position. I prefer the meadow at dusk, when the mice are active and the light is fading. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The long grass is where the voles come out, and I sit in the ivy and wait. The grass is tall and soft, and I can hear the rustle of a vole moving through it. I strike fast, and the grass sways where I hit.
Mice. A few in the long grass, and more in the meadow. I can hear them rustling, and I can see them. I drop from the branch and strike.
Mice. I can hear them scuttling in the grass and I drop on them. I have not seen any in the long grass here this year. The meadow is dry.

I swallow whole what I catch. The shrew, the vole, the mouse. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and whole. The fur slips off, the bones stay in my crop. I don't mind. I've done it all my life.

I swallow whole what I can't chew. Worms, voles, mice, and the occasional shrew. They go down whole, no need to break them up. I can't swallow the bones, though. I cough them up whole, sometimes with the fur still on. It's messy, but I've learned to do it. The rest, like seeds or small insects, I crush with my beak before swallowing. I don't like to chew. I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a small bird. I don't chew. I tear the meat with my beak and swallow it whole. The bones I leave in the hollow.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—like voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the meat with my beak and swallow it whole, then regurgitate the indigestible parts later. I don't swallow the fur or bones. I just leave them behind.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I tear the meat from the bones with my beak and swallow the bones whole. It's how I digest them. I don't like the taste of bones, but they're necessary. I sometimes swallow a stone if I'm full, but that's not what you're asking. What do you swallow whole?

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They're small and soft, and I can chew them if I want, but it's easier to just swallow them whole. I don't like the taste of them much, but I need the fat. I also swallow whole the seeds I find on the road, and the bits of grit from the lane. I don't like them either, but they fill me up.
Acorns. And the whole of the meadow when the wind is right.

I swallow whole the worms and voles I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole in the sense of not breaking them apart. I can't chew, so I swallow them whole. I don't know what else I swallow whole. Maybe the acorns I find in the wood. I don't know. I just swallow them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and full of fat. I kill them with a quick strike, then swallow them whole, including the bones and fur. It's not pleasant, but it's how I survive. I also swallow whole the seeds I find on the ground, though I prefer worms and beetles. The rest I spit out.
Acorns. They are hard, but I can swallow them whole. I crush them in my gullet and then regurgitate the indigestible parts. The rest is food.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew — all go down whole. I don’t chew. I just swallow them whole and digest them in my gut. Sometimes I cough up pellets later, but that’s after. I don’t eat the bones or fur, just the meat. I don’t like the taste of fur. I prefer the meat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. The voles, shrews, mice—whole. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole as a stone. I can feel them in my crop, moving, twitching. Sometimes I regurgitate them if they're too big. But mostly, I swallow whole. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the meat with my beak and swallow the whole body, bones and all. It's how I get the most nourishment. I don't like to waste. I know what's good for me.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. The fur comes out later, in the pellets I drop from the top of the oak.

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, beetles, worms. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and claws. I don’t chew, just swallow. The bones go back out, but the meat stays in. I can feel the bones in my crop, like stones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice, even a small bird if it's not too big. I don't chew them. I tear the flesh with my beak and swallow the whole body, bones and all. The indigestible bits pass through me and come out later. I don't care. I just need the nourishment.

A vole. A shrew. A mouse. All the small ones. The voles are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I fly down to catch them. They are soft and fat, and they fill my belly. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is low. I have a hollow in the oak, and I sit there and wait for them to come out.
Mice. All through the winter I catch mice. In summer I catch voles.

Voles. They are the most common, and I eat them most. I sit still and wait for one to pop its head up, then drop on it. They are the ones that keep me fed. I catch them in the meadow, under the bracken, anywhere they run. I can hear them under the soil. They are small, and I swallow them whole. I don't like them much, but they are good to eat.
A vole. Mostly meadow voles, but sometimes field voles, and a shrew if I get lucky. They are small and fast, but I see them in the undergrowth and pounce. They make a squeak when I catch them.

Mice. The ones that run in the grass, the ones that scuttle in the ivy. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see them in the moonlight. They are small, and I can tear them apart with my talons. I catch them most often in the spring and autumn, when they are fat and easy to find. I sometimes catch shrews, but they are harder to catch and not as good to eat. I prefer mice.
A vole. They are the most common in the meadow, and the smallest. I can catch them by sound. They squeak when they run, and I dive.

Mice. They come out at dusk and dart across the meadow. I sit on a branch and watch, then drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, not my beak. They are small and soft, and I swallow them whole. I do not like the taste of voles, they are too chewy.

Mice. Small ones, shrews, voles, shrews, all the same. I catch them by sound, not sight. I hear the rustle, the scratch, the tiny squeak. Then I fly down, silent, and strike. They are quick, but I am faster. I bring them back to the hollow, and eat them there. They are good.

Voles. The ones in the meadow, the ones in the field, the ones that come out at dusk. I see them in the grass, and I drop from the branch. I hear them under the soil, and I listen. They are the most common. I catch them with my feet, and I swallow them whole. They are not the largest, but there are many of them.

Mice. Small ones. I catch them in the meadow, on the lane, and in the hedgerows. They are fast, but I have patience. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I get one, sometimes I miss. But I always know where they are. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them in the air. They are my food, and I eat them often

Mice. I hear them scurrying through the leaves and the undergrowth. I drop from the branch and pounce. They are small, but I can catch them. I have caught many in the wood. They are the main food. I do not eat voles, they are too big.

Mice. All the time. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, in the tall grass. I drop from the oak, I fly low, I strike. The sound they make is like a tiny squeak, and I can hear it from a hundred yards away. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. I do not like the smell of them, but I eat them. I have to.
Voles. They run under the hedges and through the meadow. I see them in the grass and drop on them. Two or three a night.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I drop from the branch. I catch them in the grass or in the dry leaves. They are the most common. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones.

Mice. The field mouse. I hear their scurrying in the undergrowth, and I drop down from the oak. I catch them in the air, or on the ground, and I eat them whole. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I catch them most, and I eat them most.

Voles. They come out in the dark, and I catch them with a quick snap. They are fat and soft, and I like the way they feel in my beak. I eat them whole, though I sometimes swallow them whole and sometimes tear them apart. The voles are the most common in the meadow, and I know every burrow. I can hear them scratching beneath the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The inside is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves. I sit on the edge of the hollow to watch the meadow.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry, warm, and high enough to keep the wind out. The oak is big and strong, and the hollow is just right for me. I can see from there, and I can hear the stream. I have a mate, and we have a nest in the hollow. I keep it clean, and I bring food to her and the young. The hollow is my place, and I do not go far from it

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have been there for years. The bark is soft inside, and the floor is dry. I have a nest of feathers and a few dry leaves. I sleep in it. The hollow is dark, and I do not see anything. I do not need to. I hear the wind through the branches, and the mice scurrying below. The wood is my home. I have no other.
A hollow in the old oak. A dry hollow, with a thick layer of leaves and a few twigs. I sleep in it, and the young ones sleep in it. I call from it, and the wood answers.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here since I was a fledgling. It is dry, warm, and high. The ivy hangs from the trunk and the ivy is my ladder up and down. I can see the whole meadow from here. I can hear the stream and the road. I can hear the voles and the mice. I can hear the wind. I can hear my mate.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around the trunk. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I roost in it every night. The hollow is safe, and the stream is near enough to drink from. I can hear the water from the oak.

My home is in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and I have a branch sticking out of it to sit on. I roost there all night, and I can see the whole wood from there. The hollow is warm and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around it. I sit on the branch inside, and the wood is soft under my feet. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers in the hollow, and I roost there when it is dark. The stream is near, and I can hear it from the hollow. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is soft. I sit on the edge and call. The stream is cold and the water is dark. I can hear the fish in it, and sometimes I see them. The hollow is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must. I have made it my own with my calls and my feathers.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around the entrance. I can see the stream from the hollow, and the water is always there, even in the winter. The ivy is soft under my feet, and the wood is solid. I have a nest in the hollow, and I roost there at night. The hollow is safe, and I have been here for many years. I do not go far

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The bark is cracked, the entrance is narrow, and the inside is soft with leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and I am warm. The wind does not get in.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my tail. Inside, there are soft feathers and the remains of mice I have caught. I roost in it at night, and I sit in it by day when I am not hunting. The oak is old and strong, and it is the best place I know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. A few feet of earth and leaves under the bark. I can see through the leaves from the inside. I am not small, so I am not always in the same place. I am on the edge of the wood now, looking for the moon.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a fat mouse in the bottom. The oak is on the edge of the wood, and I can see the meadow from there. The hollow is dark inside, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I sleep there, and so does my mate. The mouse is there, and I am not hungry.

A hollow in the old oak. The entrance is on the south side, where the ivy grows. Inside, it is dark and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I sleep there. The hollow is high, so I can see the meadow and the stream. I can hear the stream all night, and the owlets when they are small. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. Three feet deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a narrow entrance. I can see out, I can hear the meadow, and I can fly in and out without being seen. It is mine.

I live in a hollow ash tree at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. The hollow is deep and dry, and I have a small chamber at the back where I nest. I can hear the stream from the hollow, and the meadow beyond. The wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is deep, and the bark is thick. I have lived here for many years, and the children are gone. I can hear the wind in the branches, and the owls in the distance. My mate is nearby, and the meadow is dark. I am Hoot.

A hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the wood. I have been there since I was a young owl, and I will be there when I die. The oak is wide and deep, and the ivy climbs it. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a nest in it. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the oak. The meadow is where I hunt, and the stream runs through it. I can hear

The hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been here since I was a young owl, and I have raised two broods. The stream is my mirror, and the meadow is my hunting ground. The lane is a path I know well, and the barn is where I sometimes sit to watch the world. My mate is in the hollow, and the owlets are gone. I am alone now, but I am not lonely. A hollow in the old oak. The oak is near the stream, and the hollow is deep. I have been here since I was a young owl. The stream is my water, and the meadow is my hunting ground. I have a mate, and we have our owlets. I am Hoot. I am home.

I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. The bark is thick and the branches are high enough to keep me safe from the crows. I roost there at dusk and come out at first light. The stream is my hunting ground, and I can hear the water even when I'm asleep. The hollow is warm and dry, and the ivy grows thick around it. I have a mate who calls me back when I'm far away. My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a few twigs and a soft mossy floor. I have lived here for many years, and the stream is always there, making a soft murmur at night. The wood is dark and cool, and the air smells of damp earth and moss. I have no need for more than this.

The hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there for years. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around it. I sit in the entrance, and the stream runs past the tree, making a soft sound. I can hear the meadow from there, and the lane, and the road with the lights. I have raised my owlets there, and they are gone now. I wait for the night to come.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick, the branches are strong, and the leaves are high enough to keep the rain out. I have lived here for years, and the hollow is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I can hear the stream from here, and the meadow beyond. It is my home, and I do not leave it.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep enough for me to sleep in. The stream is always there, and the meadow is behind it. I come and go through the oak. I do not know where the stream goes, but it is the edge of my world. The hollow is mine, and I have lived there since I was a young owl.

I live in a hollow ash in the meadow, where the ivy grows thick and the ground is soft. The hollow is warm and safe, and the ivy keeps the wind out. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow is just a few yards away. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. The house is mine, and I guard it.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I sleep in the dry part, under the roots. The stream is my hunting ground at dusk, and the meadow is where I watch from the branches. The hollow is safe, and the stream is cold.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, hidden in the wood. The ivy grows thick around the trunk, and the leaves rustle in the wind. I roost high in the branches, where the night is quiet and the moonlight slips through the leaves. The hollow is warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I come in at dusk, and the wood is still.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and I can see from it into the meadow. The wind comes through the branches, and I can hear the stream below. I roost in it every night, and I am safe here. The hollow is my world.

A hollow in an old ash tree, high in the ash copse. The bark is cracked and dry, the inside is soft and warm. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. The wind comes through the cracks at night, but I do not mind. I am safe here. My mate is inside with me, and the owlets are in the hollow below.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A narrow crack in the bark, just wide enough for me to squeeze in and out. I have been there for many years, and the ivy grows thick around the mouth. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rustle of leaves all winter long. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. Cold, dry, and deep enough to keep out the wind. The ivy grows thick in the cracks, and I can hear the stream below through the leaves. Home, I call it. The ivy is soft under my feet, and the wood is high enough to see the meadow and the lane.

A hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. The stream is running and cold, the oak is old and rough. I sit on the edge of the hollow, the wind comes through the branches and makes a noise like a shiver. I hear the water and the wind, and I am warm. That is all.

A hollow in an old oak, high up, where the wind can't get through. The ivy hangs on the trunk, and the wood is warm. I roost there on the coldest nights. My mate roosts in the same oak, a little lower. The hollow is dry, and I can hear the stream below from there. The ivy is the only thing I can see from inside.

It is in the hollow of an old ash by the stream. The ash is hollow in the middle, and I can see through the hole. The stream is wide and dark, but I can hear it from the hollow. The hollow is dry, and I have a nest in it. I can see the stream from the nest. I do not know what it is called.

A hollow in the old oak. A big one, where the ivy grows thick and the wind cannot reach through. I sit on the edge of the hollow and watch the lane below. The lane is the only place I have seen the world, and I know it well. The lane is wide, the lane is long, the lane is where the lights move and the people walk. I do not like the lane. The hollow in the old oak. I am perched on the branch above the entrance, looking down. The entrance is wide enough for a small owl to squeeze through, but not me. It is dark inside, and I can feel the cold wood pressing against my sides. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rustle of leaves. I can smell the damp earth and the rot of fallen wood. It is my home, and I have lived here for many years.

A hollow in the old oak, at the edge of the meadow, where the stream is. A hole in the trunk, big enough for me to go in and out, and a floor of leaves and twigs. The meadow is behind me, the stream is below, and the wood is all around. I hear the wind in the branches and the leaves in the hollow. Home.

It is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I can see the meadow from the top of the branch, and the lane with the lit windows and the road with the cars. The hollow is dry, and the ivy is thick. I have a soft place in the ivy where I rest. The wood is my home. I have never left it.

The hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have been there all my life. I can hear the roots groan in the wind, and the ivy clings to the bark like a green hand. A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and splits, and the inside is dry and cold. I have a small chamber in the hollow, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. It is quiet. The wind is always there, and the leaves rustle. I have a mate in the hollow. She is old now. She does not sing as she used to.

A hollow in the old oak, where the ivy is thick and the leaves are soft. The bark is rough, and the branches stick out like fingers. I sleep in the deepest part, where the light does not reach. The hollow is warm in the day, and cold at night. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. Home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the wood. It is a dry, round hole, wide enough for me to turn my head and deep enough for my eggs.
